explanation:
## How a Bonus Is Taxed

In the US, a bonus is "supplemental wages." Employers can withhold federal tax on it two ways:

- **Flat (percentage) method** — a fixed 22% federal rate on bonuses up to $1 million in a year, and 37% on the portion above $1 million. This is the most common method for a separate bonus check.
- **Aggregate method** — the bonus is lumped with your regular paycheck and withheld at your normal payroll rate, which can be higher or lower than 22%.

Withholding is not your final tax bill. It's a prepayment. Your actual liability is settled when you file, so a 22% withholding doesn't mean a 22% tax — you may get part of it back or owe more depending on your bracket.

## How This Calculator Works

**Net bonus = gross bonus × (1 − tax rate)**. Enter your gross bonus and the rate you expect to apply (22% is the default flat federal rate). The result is what lands after that income-tax withholding.

## What Else Comes Out of a Bonus

Beyond income tax, a bonus is also hit by **FICA** (7.65%: 6.2% Social Security up to the annual wage base + 1.45% Medicare, plus an extra 0.9% Medicare surtax on high earners) and, in most places, **state income tax**. To estimate your true take-home, add those to the income-tax rate you enter.

## Federal Withholding by Bonus Size (Flat Method, 2026)

Net shown is before state tax. Above $1M, the portion over the threshold is withheld at 37%. FICA is omitted on the largest rows because the Social Security base is capped, so the effective FICA rate drops.

## Why Your Refund May Differ

If your marginal bracket is below 22%, flat withholding over-collects and you get the difference back at tax time. If you're in the 24%, 32%, or higher bracket, 22% under-withholds and you'll owe the gap. High earners often adjust their W-4 to cover the shortfall instead of facing a surprise in April.

This tool is for estimation only; consult a tax professional for your exact situation. Rates reflect 2026 IRS supplemental-wage rules.

faq.q: Is my annual bonus subject to income tax?
faq.a: Yes, bonuses are taxed as ordinary income in the year you receive them, added to your total gross income.

faq.q: What withholding rate applies to bonuses?
faq.a: Federal withholding is typically 22% for bonuses up to $1 million and 37% for amounts exceeding $1 million. Your actual rate depends on your total annual income and tax bracket.

faq.q: How is my net bonus calculated?
faq.a: Net bonus = gross bonus × (1 − withholding rate). The calculator applies your specified tax rate to determine net pay.

faq.q: Does my bonus push me into a higher tax bracket?
faq.a: Potentially. Bonuses are added to your annual income, which could increase your marginal tax rate and result in more tax owed.

faq.q: What about FICA taxes (Social Security and Medicare)?
faq.a: FICA taxes (7.65% combined) also apply to bonuses in addition to income tax withholding. Your total deductions will be higher than income tax alone.

faq.q: Can I adjust my W-4 when I receive a bonus?
faq.a: Yes, you can adjust your W-4 to increase or decrease withholding to better match your expected annual tax liability.

faq.q: Should I expect additional taxes at tax time?
faq.a: Possibly. If your actual tax rate exceeds the withholding rate, you may owe additional taxes when filing your return, or you may receive a refund.

faq.q: Flat method vs aggregate method — which is better for me?
faq.a: Neither changes your final tax, only how much is withheld up front. The flat 22% method is simplest and predictable. The aggregate method withholds at your regular paycheck rate, which is lower if you're in a sub-22% bracket (more cash now, possible small bill later) and higher if you're a top earner. Employers choose the method; you can adjust your W-4 to fine-tune the result.
